subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Clipper Ship Races
description: A 60-second lesson on The Clipper Ship Races.

hook.text: In the 1860s, the first ship to deliver fresh Chinese tea to London earned the best price at auction.

buildup.text: Clipper ships raced 16,000 miles from China to London. The Great Tea Race of 1866 is the most famous.

discovery.text: Five ships left Fuzhou on the same tide. The Taeping and Ariel arrived 99 days later, 20 minutes apart.

twist.text: The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and killed clipper ships. Steamers took a shortcut they couldn't use.

climax.text: Clipper races lasted barely two decades but they produced some of the most beautiful ships ever built.

punchline.text: 16,000 miles for a cup of tea. Speed mattered that much.

quiz.question: What ended the era of clipper ship tea races?
options: The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869

details.summary: In the mid-1800s, clipper ships raced to carry the first tea of the season from China to London. The fastest ship earned the highest prices for its cargo. The Great Tea Race of 1866 between the Taeping and Ariel ended in a near-dead heat after 99 days and 14,000 miles of racing.
details.whyItMatters: The tea races captured public imagination and drove maritime innovation. They represented the peak of the sailing age before steam ships ended the competition.
takeaways: Clipper ships raced to deliver the first tea to London
The 1866 Great Tea Race was a legendary near-tie
These races drove sailing ship design to its peak

faq.question: Why did the first tea shipment command higher prices?
faq.answer: Fresh tea was considered superior, and merchants paid a premium for the first cargo to reach London. Getting to market first was a significant financial advantage. The races added excitement and publicity that further enhanced the value of the winning ship's cargo.

faq.question: What ended the clipper ship tea races?
faq.answer: The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 created a shortcut that favored steamships, which did not depend on wind. Steam-powered ships were slower per mile but more reliable and could use the canal while sailing ships could not. The era of clipper racing was essentially over by the 1870s.
